subtype: Stage 6: Owning your part, not the whole [Response]
passage: Honestly, Didi, the fight wasn't even the hard part. You know me, your little sister never backs down. The hard part was the bench behind the library, when Ritu and I finally sat down alone. I'd rehearsed a whole speech about how she started it by posting that photo. But when I opened my mouth, I just said, "I'm sorry I told everyone about your failed audition. That was mean." I didn't add "but you posted the photo." I wanted to, so badly. Ritu stared at her shoes, then said, "Kalyani, I'm sorry about the photo. I knew you'd hate it." Nobody brought up who began it. The funny thing? The next day Mehr and the others stopped taking sides too. When we cooled down, the whole group cooled down.

qa.q: Where did Kalyani and Ritu finally sit down alone?
qa.a: They sat on the bench behind the library.

qa.q: What did Kalyani want to add after the apology, and why didn't she?
qa.a: She was torn, wanting so badly to add "but you posted the photo", yet she held back because making up mattered more than proving who started it.

qa.q: Why did owning only her own part work better than demanding an apology first?
qa.a: It left Ritu free to own her part too, so neither felt forced, and the friendship came before the contest over blame.

qa.q: How did the rest of the group react once the two of them made up?
qa.a: Mehr and the others stopped taking sides the next day; when the two cooled down, the whole group did too.

grounding: Shows a teen naming her own regret without demanding the friend apologise first, and the wider group cooling once the pair does.

subtype: Stage 6: Owning your part, not the whole [Response]
passage: I'm Jai, the goalkeeper, and I watched the whole thing from the net. For a week the under-16 team had been split: Hemant's lot on one side of the dressing room, Omkar's on the other, all because of a foul in practice and a lot of shouting after. On Thursday, before warm-up, Hemant walked over to Omkar at the water tank. I couldn't hear everything. I caught "I shouldn't have shoved you," and then, after a pause, Omkar saying, "I shouldn't have called you a cheat." Neither said "you first." They shook hands, a bit awkwardly. The strange part was the rest of us. By the end of drills, people were passing across the old line like it had never been there.

qa.q: Where did Hemant walk over to Omkar?
qa.a: Hemant walked over to Omkar at the water tank before warm-up.

qa.q: What does the awkward handshake suggest about how Hemant and Omkar felt?
qa.a: They were probably still a little uncomfortable and unsure, but willing to move past who started it for the sake of the team.

qa.q: What made this repair mature rather than a standoff?
qa.a: Each named what they regretted, the shove and the insult, without saying "you first", so nobody had to win.

qa.q: How did the split team experience the two of them making up?
qa.a: Jai and the others relaxed; by the end of drills people were passing across the old line as if it had never been there. 🙂

grounding: Shows two teens each owning their part without insisting on who started it, and the divided team cooling when they do.
